items.titel: LUCAS Drones To Be Built In Containerized Robotic Micro Factories Designed To Be Forward Deployed
items.anriss: A California robotics company called Machina has been issued a $9 million award for a containerized system to robotically mass-produce Low-Cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System (LUCAS) airframes close to the point of need. As TWZ has …

absaetze.t: A California robotics company called Machina has been issued a $9 million award for a containerized system to robotically mass-produce Low-Cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System (LUCAS) airframes close to the point of need. As TWZ has frequently noted, LUCAS drones, and one-way attack weapons like them, are playing an increasing role in U.S. combat operations and military planning.

The award to Machina is the latest example of the Pentagon’s push to use containerized 3D printing and other advanced fabricating systems closer to the front lines to shorten supply chains that could get severely degraded in a major conflict. Decentralizing production of drones also allows units to be more flexible and tailor their own production to their specific needs at any given moment. For instance, a unit can produce variations of multiple designs that are best suited to an upcoming mission instead of having to use whatever they are shipped.

This 18-month contract from the Defense Department’s Organic Industrial Base Modernization Challenge calls for Machina to prove it can build LUCAS drones at deployed locations with its RoboCraftsman system, Ed Mehr, founder and CEO of Machina, told TWZ Friday afternoon. A decision on producing them at scale in many other locales will come later.

Creating containerized production of drones and components using 3D printing and other advanced manufacturing techniques at the forward edge is a burgeoning industry. The Machina system is one of a rapidly growing number of capabilities built around this concept, although many focus on smaller drones.
Building Drones Near The Point Of Need

Initially, the plan calls for Machina to set up so-called “Edge Factories” at two locations in the continental United States, said Mehr. However, the ultimate goal is to be able to deploy them to forward locations in countries like Kuwait.

The Edge Factories consist of the company’s containerized RoboCraftsman manufacturing cells, Mehr told us. A 20-foot by 36-foot system that weighs 120,000 pounds fully installed, it is essentially two robotic arms that form the airframe out of metal using reductive manufacturing based on a variety of requirements. Payload weight, range and other factors are punched into a software system designed by the nTop company and the robotic arms then cut the metal into the desired form factor based on the required specifications.

Machina uses metal instead of composites that many drones are made out of because “not only it is cheaper, it is more widely available and now can be processed with an automated process like ours versus composites, which are all done by hand layup,” Mehr explained.
The following Machina video shows how the RoboCraftsman system, guided by the inputs, forms the metal to craft the airframe.
This avoids having to use equipment like dies and rolls, dramatically speeding the process and allowing production at scale, Mehr stated.

“Basically, the agentic AI agents can explore and generate whole different versions of an airframe with different parameters,” Mehr proffered. “Because now it’s parameterized, you can just change the parameters and you get another airframe, and then evaluate if that airframe is good for the requirement they want.”

This way, the RoboCraftsman system “can easily generate 20, 30, 40, 50 different designs just in software, and then put it through simulations to figure out which one actually meets the requirement for that,” the Machina CEO added.

“The concept is that we’re going to bring this capability closer to the point of need, so that you can build a different requirement for let’s say PACOM versus U.S. CENTCOM versus in Ukraine,” Mehr said. “They can easily switch and build a drone that they need.”

Under this contract, each Edge Factory will consist of one or two RoboCraftsman cells and each cell can make a LUCAS airframe in two to five days, depending on the size, Mehr said. A scaled deployment of 10 or more cells would take place under a new contract, he added.
The systems can make “anywhere from a one-off all the way to the thousands, sometimes tens of thousands,” Mehr said. It all depends on the number of RoboCraftsman systems that are ordered.

At the moment, Mehr envisions that each 12-foot airframe will cost “somewhere around $15,000 to $40,000,” depending on the complexity. This range is a relatively common price point for Russian Shahed-136 variants and U.S. knockoffs under the LUCAS program.
The company has already produced a six-foot, half-scale airframe that was recently tested at Edwards Air Force Base, said Mehr. However, that initial test proved problematic.

“The first design had some challenges with crosswind mitigation,” Mehr told us. “Since then, we have moved the location of the engine slightly to enable better crosswind mitigation, and now we’re running again. And the beauty is for us to go from one design to the next is just like a couple of months, a maximum of three months. Like we can just then try it again.”

Mehr said that Machina is not working with SpektreWorks, which designed and made the LUCAS drones previously supplied to the U.S. military and already used in combat. SpektreWorks declined to comment.
The Edge Factory contract is one of several Machina has been awarded to use these systems to help build and repair military hardware.
In July, Machina was issued a qualification contract by Lockheed Martin to produce fuel tanks for AGM-158 Joint Air-To-Surface Standoff Missiles (JASSM).

That plan called for the creation of a 200,000-square-foot facility “designed to house up to 50 RoboCraftsman cells and support high-rate production of mission-critical metal structures for defense programs including JASSM,” according to a media release at the time. “By integrating forming, machining, welding, and assembly under one roof, Machina Factory 3 compresses production timelines from months to days.”

“Lockheed Martin Ventures invested in Machina Labs for its powerful combination of speed, flexibility, and scalability, and our teams have worked closely to transition key capabilities to production,” said Chris Moran, vice president and general manager, Lockheed Martin Ventures. “Machina’s work advances capacity, reduces risk, and helps ensure we can deliver mission-critical capabilities at scale. We congratulate Machina on this milestone as a supplier, which further strengthens an innovative and resilient American Defense Industrial Base.”
Earlier this year, a Machina RoboCraftsman platform helped repair a C-17 Globemaster III cargo jet that was damaged during a tornado, Mehr told us.

The system “fabricated a first-of-its-kind replacement part for the damaged C-17 without the need for dedicated tooling,” the company noted. “Machina deployed a RoboCraftsman at the RSO [Rapid Sustainment Office], where production for a left nose panel began in March 2026 and was completed in May 2026. The aircraft returned to flight on July 30, 2026 at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio.”
We asked the Pentagon for information about why they selected Machina and their metrics for success, but we have not heard back yet.
Pentagon Pushing For Deployable Manufacturing

The U.S. military has been pushing for several years for the employment of mobile additive and other forms of advanced manufacturing “to produce unmanned aircraft components in remote or austere environments and reduce dependence on traditional supply chains,” the Air Force’s innovation arm, AFWERX, noted last month.
The idea is to place these systems in a wide array of locations, produce the quantity needed and tailor the airframe for the mission.

In one such case, the Air National Guard and Air Force Special Operations Command partnered with the San Diego-based Firestorm company in 2023 “to create an expeditionary assembly unit capable of mass-producing unmanned aerial systems,” according to the Pentagon.
The result was called an Expeditionary Manufacturing Cell or xCell.

“It’s basically an expeditionary 3D printer,” Master Sgt. Richard Stone, 194th Air Support Operations Group innovation officer, explained at the time. “The basis of the technology is … it’s about the size of a [shipping container] and it can print out, for this specific use case, drones.”
“Inside this [shipping container], it’ll print out all the components,” said Stone “But then you have what’s called RPA, which is robotic process [automation.]”
The xCell “prints the individual pieces and then uses RPA to assemble the major components of the drone,” the Pentagon added.

“The user can take these components and, almost like Legos, put them together,” said Stone. “So if you want a longer drone with a specific payload, you can take those components and put them together and the computer will tell you, ‘This is where the wings go and this is where the center of gravity should be.”

The company went on to produce Tempest drones that were flying with 3rd Littoral Combat Team, 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment, during Exercise Balikatan 2026 at Cagayan North International Airport in the Philippines, AFWERX noted.
Our own Jamie Hunter recently interviewed Craig Anders, senior vice president of growth at Aevex, about the company’s ForgeX containerized 3D drone printing system.

The ForgeX system “represents being able to take the fight further forward, print drones on demand, print them out towards the front of the lines, cut down the logistics trail, and absolutely revolutionize the battlefield,” said Anders.

The goal is to be “able to kick these planes out the door on short timelines to go out and get the missions done, work within the local area to make sure that the mission can be accomplished by any means necessary,” he added.
Anders said the ForgeX printers fabricate three types of drones, the Vandal, Onyx and Raker. He added that the system can produce up to 880 a year.
Growing U.S. Reliance On LUCAS

The U.S. military first announced it had begun fielding LUCAS, which was reverse-engineered from the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, in December 2025. This came just months after TWZ laid out a detailed case for why the U.S. military should start acquiring Shahed-136 clones in large volumes. LUCAS made its official combat debut in the opening phases of major combat operations against Iran earlier this year. The pusher-propeller, combustion-engine-powered kamikaze drones were first launched from the ground, a U.S. official told us at the time. They can also be fired from ships. In March, CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper told us the LUCAS drones were “indispensable.”
The following video shows Cooper answering our question about the LUCAS drones.

Now the Army is looking to expand the use of these weapons to the Pacific, Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, head of the 7th Infantry Division, told us during the Association of the U.S. Army (AUSA) conference last month.

“So we see that playing a key role in order to be able to achieve that effect at mass, … [and] in an affordable manner, while also being able potentially to preserve something that’s more exquisite for something that requires an exquisite munition.”

“So as we start modeling out what it looks like to be able to penetrate a portion of the anti-access/area denial network in support of the joint task force in the PACOM [U.S. Pacific Command] area of operations, we started looking at, well, how do I bend – how do I achieve mass at a cost curve?” the 7th Infantry and MDC-PAC commander explained. “What effect am I really trying to achieve on a system in order to provide that window of opportunity for that joint force commander?”

“So maybe I don’t necessarily need to sink a ship, but if I take out certain systems on that vessel, well then it creates this temporal window opportunity,” he continued. “Then that joint force commander can surge in that carrier strike group or bomber task force.”

items.titel: Estimé jusqu’à 5 millions de livres, un paysage oublié d’un maître de la Renaissance réapparaît après 70 ans : « l’une des découvertes les plus passionnantes »
items.anriss: Une forêt profonde, un ciel chargé de nuages et un arc-en-ciel qui perce la lumière… Ce petit tableau d’à peine 23 centimètres de haut pourrait bien constituer l’une des redécouvertes majeures de l’année sur le marché de l’art. Signée du …

absaetze.t: Resté dans une collection privée suisse pendant 70 ans, un rare paysage d’Albrecht Altdorfer, figure majeure de la Renaissance allemande, sera mis en vente chez Sotheby’s à Londres le 9 décembre. Son estimation atteint 3 à 5 millions de livres sterling.

Une forêt profonde, un ciel chargé de nuages et un arc-en-ciel qui perce la lumière… Ce petit tableau d’à peine 23 centimètres de haut pourrait bien constituer l’une des redécouvertes majeures de l’année sur le marché de l’art. Signée du monogramme d’Albrecht Altdorfer (vers 1480-1538) et réalisée autour de 1520, cette peinture à l’huile sur parchemin, marouflé sur un panneau de bois, n’avait pas été montrée au public depuis sept décennies. Seules deux autres peintures de l’artiste représentant exclusivement un paysage étaient connues. L’œuvre sera mise en vente chez Sotheby’s, à Londres, le 9 décembre prochain.
Un tableau d’Albrecht Altdorfer réapparaît après 70 ans

Intitulée Paysage très boisé avec un arc-en-ciel derrière les arbres, un éperon rocheux au loin à droite, sous un ciel chargé de nuages (A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky), l’œuvre a été réalisée vers 1520. Elle était conservée depuis 1957 dans une collection privée suisse, après avoir appartenu aux comtes de Harrach, une famille aristocratique dont la collection était installée au palais Harrach, à Vienne. Le père de l’actuel propriétaire l’avait acquise cette année-là. Depuis, le tableau est resté hors de la vue du public.

Albrecht Altdorfer, Paysage boisé avec un arc-en-ciel derrière les arbres et un éperon rocheux au loin à droite, sous un ciel chargé de nuages, vers 1520, huile sur parchemin collé sur bois, 23,4 x 19,8 cm. Estimation : 3 à 5 millions de livres. © Sotheby’s

Sa redécouverte et son identification, au début de l’année 2026, ont suscité l’enthousiasme des spécialistes. George Gordon, coprésident du département mondial des maîtres anciens chez Sotheby’s, y voit « l’une des découvertes les plus passionnantes que l’on puisse imaginer » dans le domaine. L’estimation annoncée, comprise entre 3 et 5 millions de livres sterling, reflète la rareté de cette peinture autant que l’importance de son auteur.
Altdorfer, un pionnier du paysage autonome à la Renaissance

Né vers 1480 à Ratisbonne, en Bavière, Albrecht Altdorfer appartient aux grandes figures de la Renaissance allemande. Peintre, dessinateur et graveur, il est traditionnellement associé à l’École du Danube, un courant qui se développe au début du XVIe siècle dans les régions bavaroises et autrichiennes traversées par le fleuve. Chez ces artistes, la nature acquiert une place nouvelle : les forêts, les reliefs et les phénomènes atmosphériques ne servent plus seulement de décor aux scènes religieuses ou historiques.

Albrecht Altdorfer, Paysage au grand épicéa, vers 1520, eau-forte aquarellée, Albertina, Vienne, présentée dans l’exposition « Albrecht Altdorfer. Maître de la Renaissance allemande » au musée du Louvre en 2020 © Connaissance des Arts / Anne-Sophie Lesage-Münch

Altdorfer pousse cette attention jusqu’à faire du paysage un sujet à part entière. Après avoir commencé sa carrière par le dessin et la gravure, il se tourne vers la peinture de paysages autour de 1511, probablement marqué par un voyage dans les Alpes. Il compte parmi les premiers artistes européens à consacrer des œuvres autonomes à la représentation de la nature. Albrecht Dürer (1471-1528) avait certes réalisé des paysages à l’aquarelle dès la fin du XVe siècle, mais ceux-ci étaient principalement conçus comme des études préparatoires. Altdorfer, lui, fait du paysage une composition achevée. L’importance de son œuvre a été mise en lumière au musée du Louvre, qui lui a consacré une exposition rétrospective en 2020, en collaboration avec l’Albertina de Vienne.
Un troisième paysage à l’huile pour le maître allemand

Jusqu’à cette redécouverte, seules deux autres peintures à l’huile d’Altdorfer représentant exclusivement un paysage étaient connues : Paysage avec une passerelle, conservé à la National Gallery de Londres, et Paysage du Danube près de Ratisbonne, à l’Alte Pinakothek de Munich. Cette troisième composition vient donc enrichir un corpus particulièrement restreint.
Albrecht Altdorfer, Paysage du Danube près de Ratisbonne, vers 1528-1530, Alte Pinakothek, Munich © Wikimedia Commons

De petit format, l’œuvre est dominée par une forêt dense, dont les arbres et les sous-bois occupent presque toute la surface. Aucun personnage ne vient animer la scène. À droite, un éperon rocheux se détache au loin, tandis qu’un arc-en-ciel apparaît derrière les arbres, sous un ciel chargé de nuages. La lumière, filtrée par les frondaisons, donne à cette nature foisonnante une dimension à la fois poétique et mystérieuse. Altdorfer ne cherche pas seulement à restituer un paysage : il en fait une expérience visuelle, où la végétation, le ciel et les variations lumineuses composent une atmosphère singulière. Cette attention à la puissance expressive de la nature trouvera des échos, plusieurs siècles plus tard, dans les paysages des peintres romantiques allemands.
Un événement sur le marché des maîtres anciens

La dernière transaction importante concernant une peinture d’Altdorfer remonte à 1980, lorsque la National Gallery de Londres acquiert Le Christ faisant ses adieux à sa mère (vers 1520). L’œuvre avait alors fait l’objet d’une transaction privée, conclue avec les ayants droit du collectionneur Julius Wernher. Selon Sotheby’s, aucune peinture de l’artiste n’aurait depuis été proposée aux enchères. L’absence de référence récente rend donc l’estimation de ce paysage particulièrement délicate, la maison de vente en attend entre 3 et 5 millions de livres sterling.
Albrecht Altdorfer, Le Christ faisant ses adieux à sa mère, vers 1520, National Gallery de Londres © Wikimedia Commons

Altdorfer occupe une place de premier plan dans la peinture allemande du XVIe siècle, même si sa notoriété demeure moins immédiate que celle d’Albrecht Dürer ou de Lucas Cranach l’Ancien (1472-1553). Il a pourtant bénéficié de commandes prestigieuses, notamment celle du duc Guillaume IV de Bavière pour La Bataille d’Alexandre à Issos, achevée en 1529 et aujourd’hui conservée à l’Alte Pinakothek. Il travaille pour l’empereur Maximilien Ier à Innsbruck, à partir de 1513, avant de revenir à Ratisbonne durant la Réforme, où il meurt en 1538.
Albrecht Altdorfer, La Bataille d’Alexandre, 1529, Alte Pinakothek, Munich © Wikimedia Commons

Le tableau redécouvert sera présenté lors de la vente « Old Master & 19th Century Paintings Evening Auction » aux côtés d’une vue de Rome peinte par Joseph Mallord William Turner, dont Sotheby’s n’a pas communiqué l’estimation. Avant la vacation londonienne, il sera exposé dans les salles de la maison de ventes à New York, puis à Londres.

items.titel: Swedish museums restitute objects to Nigeria and Bolivia
items.anriss: The objects being returned from museums in Stockholm and Gothenburg include Benin bronzes looted by British troops in 1897 and pre-Colombian sacred objects robbed from graves near La Paz in the 1970s

absaetze.t: Swedish museums last week began returning dozens of statues stolen by British troops from the Kingdom of Benin as well as sacred objects looted by grave robbers in the 1970s in Bolivia.

Three years after the Swedish government—at the time backed by the far-right Sweden Democrats—agreed to two restitution requests, the National Museums of World Culture (SMVK) began the final phases of enacting them.

At a ceremony in Lagos, 39 Benin objects were formally restituted to Nigeria, while according to Swedish media, 77 objects from the Niño Korin village—including the skull of a Kallawaya healer— were taken from storage in Gothenburg to be transported to the National Museum of Archaeology in La Paz.
The Bolivian objects, dating to around 600 to 1000 AD, the Tiwanku period, were looted by locals in grave robberies in the 1970s and were later sold to the museum, according to the SMVK website.

The African objects are some of thousands that were violently looted by British troops in 1897 from the Edo people in the old Kingdom of Benin, located in what is now Nigeria. They were later acquired by the former Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm. Six will remain in Sweden as part of a ten-year loan.

The restitution process began, according to the SMVK, after “clear signals from the Nigerian authority, the National Commission for Museums and Monuments, that they would welcome the return of all objects.”

Michael Barrett, the curator for Africa at SMVK, was in Lagos for the ceremonial signing-over of the 39 cultural objects, known as Emwin Arre. “I hope [this] is part of a broader shift in how our museums relate to the world around us,” he tells The Art Newspaper on his return.

“For too long colonial legacies of violence, theft, and exploitation have stood in the way of museum practices that are more responsive to a wider set of stakeholders, not least communities who have cultural and historical ties to our collections. Returning violently looted belongings to their communities of origin is a necessary first step.”

The process, he adds, is also part of earning the trust of modern audiences. “A focus on these relationships must be a central part of our practice going forward,” he adds. “At least if museums with ‘world collections’ are ever to live up to their potential [as] places where visitors may learn about humanity’s cultural achievements and many ways of being- in-the-world, in an environment defined by respect, empathy and curiosity.”

The Swedish restitutions follow a trend among European countries to return art and objects looted or obtained unethically from around the world. In 2022, Germany handed over a substantial collection of Benin bronzes to Nigeria. The Netherlands returned 119 similar objects in 2025 and the Dutch Museum de Fundatie returned an additional Benin bronze plaque last month.

While Cambridge University returned legal ownership of its collection of 116 objects to Nigeria in February, the British Museum last year ruled out the imminent restitution of stolen treasures, suggesting “collaboration” instead.

Staffan Lundén, researcher at the University of Gothenburg’s School of Global Studies, has studied the topic of “dealing with difficult pasts” and the British Museum’s collection of objects looted in Benin City. He says, by contrast, these restitutions were largely depoliticised in Sweden. “The decision was taken by the right-wing government,” he points out. “It is seen as common sense, moral justice and in line with the Swedish self-perception of being a progressive country which takes international responsibility.”

items.titel: Andy Warhol's Habibi Phase in Kuwait
items.anriss: VENICE — In January 1977, Andy Warhol skipped President Jimmy Carter’s inauguration to spend a week attending tea parties and dinners in Kuwait. He was invited by the country's national arts council and held a solo exhibition at the Salat …

absaetze.t: Raed Yassin's exhibition “Warhol of Arabia” reimagines the pop artist's 1977 visit to the Gulf country and a bygone era in the Middle East.
November 9, 2026 — 4 min read

VENICE — In January 1977, Andy Warhol skipped President Jimmy Carter’s inauguration to spend a week attending tea parties and dinners in Kuwait. He was invited by the country's national arts council and held a solo exhibition at the Salat Al Funoon gallery, featuring portraits of Mao Zedong and Marilyn Monroe and an array of flower prints. Domestically, his star was fading; with fewer patrons willing to meet his high asking prices, Warhol was under pressure to enter new markets. In Kuwait, where the recent oil boom had brought an influx of cash and a tether to the West and its cultural exports, he found more than a few interested buyers.

Nearly 50 years later, contemporary artist Raed Yassin has mounted a selection of photographic mixed-media works for the 61st Venice Biennale’s main exhibition, In Minor Keys, inventing scenes from that trip from the perspective of a fly on the wall.

“Warhol of Arabia” (all works 2016–2018) uses a real event as its anchor to paint a rich fiction using Pop aesthetics. In “The Party XII,” Warhol is depicted on the floor between a sheikh and a stylish kaftaned woman; Yassin painted only Warhol in color, making his hair pink and his glasses yellow, marking him as an outsider. “The Exhibition XIII” stamps four primary-colored headscarves onto a photo of Warhol with his Campbell’s soup can multiples, modifying the super-Western imagery the artist typically favored.

“The Gulf region in the 70s was kind of a black hole. No one knew what was going on, especially culturally,” Yassin told Hyperallergic. “You hear about oil and that kind of industry, but I was interested in what was beyond, what was happening in society. This is my imagination of it, which creates a different world entirely.”

items.titel: The Big Review: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous ★★★★½
items.anriss: A gorgeous and largely convincing exhibition that reveals a clear codependency between the two artists

absaetze.t: Total star rating: ★★★★½
The works: ★★★★★The show: ★★★★

He was Jack the Dripper. She was The Wife. That is how it went for artist couples in gender-coded mid-century America (and elsewhere). Yet, Lee Krasner (1908-84) played more than a supporting role in her decade-long marriage to Jackson Pollock (1912-56). When his work eclipsed hers, she remained as committed to her own painting as she was to every aspect of his life—except his infidelity and the alcoholism that in 1956 drove him to his death. Even then, she put her devotion to consequential use in securing his legacy. Now the time has come to fully appreciate hers.
Signature Pollocks ricochet off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa

That is the organising principle behind Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, the gorgeous and largely convincing blockbuster at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. While other US museums have previously surveyed the artists separately and in tandem, for the Met curators David Breslin and Brinda Kumar, none gave Krasner, a first-generation Abstract Expressionist, a fair shake.

Their exhibition strives to give a primacy to Krasner’s work that parallels Pollock’s. Note whose name comes first in the show’s title. Its subtitle likewise derives from a Krasner at the she-who-laughs-last finale. What’s more, a dramatically lit, black box of a gallery starts it off with a bracing presentation of six vertical abstractions that Krasner made in the 1950s by collaging cuttings from her unsold paintings with pieces of canvas and bits of Pollock’s drawings punctuated by slashes of pink and orange.

Nonetheless, the eye keeps moving to a window-like opening that functions as a proscenium for the theatre of Pollock’s Convergence: No. 10 (1952), an immense and riveting painting of black paint skeins shot with explosions of colour. Mounted on an angled, freestanding wall in another room, the sight offers viewers a taste of what is in store: signature Pollocks ricocheting off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa.

If only the curators did not show Krasner still riding his coattails. Pollock’s name remains the bigger draw. Ultimately, he still comes off as the bigger trailblazer, and she, his foremost champion, more willing to risk failure to experiment and invent. As Breslin speculated during the press preview: “I don’t think we would have a Jackson Pollock if it weren’t for what Krasner did to support his work.”

There is no way to test that theory, but if Krasner and Pollock proves anything, it is that the artists’ relationship was so codependent that the reverse may be just as true. Yet, today her influence and market value pale before his. Krasner’s auction record, set at Sotheby’s in 2019, is $11.7m for The Eye is the First Circle (1960), one of her larger canvases in the show. That is not chump change, but this year Christie’s sold Pollock’s Number 7A (1948) for $181.2m, an eye-watering price but still short of the reported $200m that financier Ken Griffin paid David Geffen, in 2016, for Number 17A (also 1948).
She was better-known

Krasner and Pollock met in 1942, when she was better-known to the Abstract Expressionist crowd in New York and Pollock the only unfamiliar name in a show of American and European Modernists (partially recreated at the Met) that the painter John Graham organised and included works by both. By linking their small, vibrant abstractions with works by Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Henri Matisse, Amadeo Modigliani, Giorgio de Chirico and Willem de Kooning, the show virtually jumpstarted their careers. It also made them a couple.

Krasner introduced herself in a spontaneous visit to Pollock’s studio and was so dazzled that she hit a creative block. That did not stop them from dating. He was a Midwestern former student of Thomas Hart Benton in thrall to Picasso and Mexican muralists. She was inspired by Arshile Gorky’s abstractions and Matisse’s cut-outs. Soon he was importing a Matissean palette to his painting and showing at Peggy Guggenheim’s Art of this Century gallery. Sales were not brisk. Pollock’s drinking was more prodigious. Krasner insisted they marry and move to Springs, in East Hampton—to protect him from himself—and persuaded Guggenheim to cover the downpayment.

Relocating did the trick for three unusually sober years—long enough for Pollock to produce his breakthrough drip paintings and achieve lasting fame, before settling, intermittently, into new bouts of alcoholism and depression; a creative paralysis set in. Krasner’s career took off, with a confident 1955 solo show at New York’s Stable Gallery.

Breslin and Kumar take care not to place the artists’ works close together, so Krasner’s modestly-scaled paintings can hook the eye without being overwhelmed by Pollock’s volatile monumentalism. Until she was widowed and took over Pollock’s now-famous barn, Krasner worked in their kitchen and he in an upstairs bedroom. Two contiguous galleries, both painted black, approximate the size of the artists’ studios and distill the show’s thesis with luminous economy, leading viewers from the lyrical, early choreography of his pours, drips and stains to her smaller but exquisite Little Images—mosaic-like geometries painted with a palette knife.

From these sepulchral chambers the show opens to a large, high-ceilinged gallery flooded with daylight from newly revealed windows on Central Park. Here, Convergence hangs, backed with the Met’s prize Pollock, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950). The operatic shift in tone and scale drives home the outsize renown Pollock achieved after a 1949 feature in Life magazine posed the question, “Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?”

In the same gallery, tellingly, the eight collage paintings Krasner showed at Stable Gallery turn from the Pollocks to face each other like the stones of Stonehenge and look just as ritualistic, if more elated. After that, it’s back to black for a segment titled Re:Echo (after a Krasner), where Pollock’s arabesque, later works hang near her Robert Motherwell-like abstractions of the same period.

The rest of the show is all Krasner, but she outlived Pollock by 28 years. The swirling, abstracted floral landscapes became monumental, but appear in a few too many galleries, homogenizing their visual impact. The point—that no full understanding of one artist can come without the other—has already been made, capped by the one side-by-side juxtaposition: The Deep (1953), a chilling canvas where Pollock nearly obliterated a dark biomorph in clouds of white, and Birth (1956), an image of interlocking pink and black forms that Krasner painted the year he died. That pairing said it all.
Will this show correct a historic imbalance? Probably not market-wise, but a reputational correction seems both necessary and likely.
Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, until 31 January 2027
Curators: David Breslin and Brinda Kumar
Tickets: $30 (concessions available)
What the other critics said

The New York Times’s Holland Cotter describes the exhibition as an “exercise of art-historical reset”, and calls its installation of Pollocks “an entrancing sight”, while exulting in the “distinctive impression of personal joy” in Krasner’s post-Pollock work. In The Wall Street Journal, Karen Wilkin applauds the curators for encouraging “concentration on their work, rather than the mythology attached to both painters”, and on her Instagram, Jasper Johns’s biographer Deborah Solomon raves: “It’s like holding two opposed thoughts in your brain at the same time and wondering if your head will explode from the exhilaration of it all.”
